comment.value: The reviewers agree that this paper makes a timely and impactful contribution by introducing AnomalyCoT, a multimodal Chain-of-Thought dataset for industrial anomaly detection (IAD). The dataset addresses critical gaps in existing resources by providing structured reasoning processes, diverse scenarios, and precise anomaly localization. The proposed data generation pipeline ensures accurate and interpretable CoT annotations, enabling unique evaluation of MLLMs’ reasoning in IAD. The authors conduct comprehensive experiments across commercial and open-source models, with results showing substantial performance gains, which highlights the dataset’s practical utility. Overall, the paper is well-executed, clearly demonstrates novelty, and offers a valuable benchmark for advancing multimodal reasoning in IAD.

Thanks for the follow-up questions!

Yes, I will provide you with more details of the experiment. We conducted the human expert experiment using all the test samples from the fine-tuning experiment. To fully reflect the researchers' capabilities and knowledge in industrial anomaly detection tasks and highlight the differences in learning patterns between humans and MLLMs before officially performing the tasks, we chose to only retain the test questions and options without setting additional prompts. At the same time, we ensured that the experts had not reviewed the corresponding ground truth samples before the test. In fact, we also built a simple  answer interface to avoid the experts making mistakes due to other factors during the test and to facilitate the statistics of the time consumed and the submitted answers after the test. Lastly, the accuracy rate of the expert test reached 62.67%, and the average time spent on each question was approximately 5 seconds. Please note that the experts  also generated thought chains during the thinking process of the test, but they were not explicitly expressed. For the potential biases that may exist in the experiment, we will conduct a thorough discussion in subsequent more comprehensive experiments.

We appreciate your high quality review and the positive score. Below we will reply to your comments.

***Regarding the human expert performance.***

The reviewer pointed out a very good point. In fact, we particularly agree with comparing the MLLMs after learning CoT with human experts to clearly and intuitively demonstrate the practical significance of the accuracy of the fine-tuned model. Therefore, we invited an industrial anomaly detection researcher as an expert to conduct human evaluation on 7,916 questions in the test set. As shown in the following table, the human expert outperformed the ordinary model by 17.14\%, and the best model outperformed the human expert by 34.79\%, highlighting the outstanding performance of the model fully learning CoT reasoning in challenging IAD tasks and further revealing the excellent potential of our work in future anomaly detection tasks. Thank you for pointing this out, and we will provide a more comprehensive supplement in the next version.
| **Method**                  | **Accuracy** |
|-----------------------------|:------------:|
| Human (expert)               | 62.67        |
| Qwen2.5-VL (Pre-trained)     | 45.53        |
| Qwen2.5-VL (Full)            | 97.46        |

***Regarding the potential limitation.***

We agree with your point. Although specific reasoning requirements and key visual information are incorporated into the prompts, errors may still occur due to variations in inference styles across the model series. Avoiding this potential limitation not only requires a more complete prompt but also a more thorough comparison experiment. We believe this is an interesting and promising future research direction.

Thanks again for the high-quality review. We hope our response could address your main concerns and we are happy to answer any further questions.

We appreciate your high quality review and the positive score. Below we will reply to your comments.

***This paper focuses on MLLMs but lacks comparison with state-of-the-art traditional IAD methods, which could better contextualize the dataset's impact on the field.***

This is a very good question. 

We used the representative traditional IAD methods SPADE, PaDiM, and PatchCore to conduct experiments on the most well-known IAD dataset, MVTec AD, and selected Llama 3.2-Vision, which performed best in the LoRA fine-tuning experiment, as the MLLM for comparison. The corresponding results of each method are shown in the following table. Since most traditional IAD methods focus on whether anomalies occur within the scene and calculate the anomaly probability of the output image, Image-AUC is used as the main metric, and it is difficult to obtain the classification accuracy due to the limitation of performing defect classification tasks. However, MLLMs can not only complete general anomaly detection tasks but also handle complex defect classification tasks and directly output the answer to the problem, making accuracy the most intuitive evaluation metric. The specific comparison between these two types of methods using different key indicators is a very interesting question, and we will discuss it more fully in the next version.
| Method                  | **Image-AUC** | **Accuracy** |
| :---------------------- | :-----------: | :----------: |
| SPADE                   |     85.42     |      -       |
| PaDiM                   |     90.56     |      -       |
| PatchCore               |     98.81     |      -       |
| Llama 3.2-Vision (LoRA) |       -       |    87.65     |
| Llama 3.2-Vision (Full) |       -       |    97.26     |

***While integrating multiple datasets, the paper does not explicitly address potential biases in source data distributions, which may affect generalizability to certain industrial sectors.***

Yes, you are correct. It appears we did not conduct a detailed discussion in the main text regarding potential biases in the source data distribution. However, in Table 6 of Appendix G, we present the specific results of Llama 3.2-Vision in all sub-dataset scenarios. We found that after LoRA/Full fine-tuning, the lowest accuracy in the sub-datasets reached 78.39\%, while the highest accuracy even reached 100\%, indicating that the fine-tuned model performed well in different scenarios.

To fully demonstrate the generalization ability of the model after learning the dataset, we selected four representative IAD datasets (MVTec AD, MVTec LOCO AD, VisA, and GoodsAD) from all sub-datasets and used the remaining sub-datasets to fine-tune the model to reasonably test its generalization ability. The model still chose Llama 3.2-Vision. Additionally, we conducted a generalization ablation study without CoT to assess its impact on model generalization capability. Domain knowledge was incorporated both before fine-tuning and after fine-tuning to perform comparative experiments. The experimental results are shown in the following table. We found that the model still achieved good accuracy in unseen scenarios after fine-tuning, indicating that the learned model achieved excellent generalization ability.

|                      |  **CoT**  | **w.o. CoT** |
| :------------------- | :-------: | :----------: |
| **Pre-trained**      |   46.18   |    35.75     |
| **Pre-trained + dm** |   38.12   |    29.32     |
| **LoRA**             |   70.37   |  **62.97**   |
| **LoRA+dm**          | **75.78** |    50.76     |

We then fine-tuned the model using the remaining scene data to reasonably test its generalization ability. The model selected was Llama 3.2-Vision, which performed best in the LoRA fine-tuning experiment. Additionally, we conducted a generalization ablation study without CoT to assess its impact on the model's generalization capability. Domain knowledge was incorporated both before fine-tuning and after fine-tuning to perform comparative experiments. As shown in the table below, the fine-tuned model maintained strong accuracy in unseen scenarios while demonstrating significant improvement compared to fine-tuning without CoT. These results collectively indicate that the fine-tuned model possesses superior generalization capability, and that the implementation of CoT substantially enhances the model's generalization ability. We also noticed an interesting point that only the fine-tuned model with CoT improved its performance after adding domain knowledge. We will clarify the meaning of our results more clearly in the next version.

| :------------------- | :-------: | :----------: |
| **Pre-trained**      |   46.18   |    35.75     |

| **LoRA**             |   70.37   |  **62.97**   |
| **LoRA+dm**          | **75.78** |    50.76     |

> *Notations: dm stands for domain knowledge.*

***The paper describes a “substantial growth” in data scale (line 71); yet, in terms of number of samples the authors mostly combine existing datasets.***

This is a very good question. 

Our description of the data scale in the paper may not have emphasized the key points. In practice, while the majority of image samples in the dataset originate from public datasets, the primary chain-of-thought annotations for each sample were constructed and tailored by us. Furthermore, all annotations for the anomalous samples were manually and uniformly labeled, deliberately avoiding the use of existing dataset annotations to prevent format inconsistency issues. At the same time, our independently collected "Self" dataset also contains 8,466 image samples, which account for a certain proportion of the total samples. Finally, detailed information about each sub-dataset can be found in Appendix A.

***Some parts of the writing are less clear. E.g., lines 91-95; 104-106; 121-122; 224-227. Also figure 2 is hard to comprehend.***

First, we politely point out that in lines 91 to 95 of the paper, the specific expression means that we used the QwenVL-Max model and combined it with a prompt containing the specific coordinates of the anomalous area, the defect type of the current sample, and the basic framework of reasoning to generate the initial CoT. After an initial manual inspection, we found the erroneous data in the generated CoT and summarized their characteristics, and then set up a corresponding filtering mechanism to update and iterate the incorrect examples. After the iteration was completed, we conducted another manual inspection of the CoT data to ensure its accuracy.

Second, regarding the expression in lines 104 to 106 of the paper, it mainly means that we conducted an ablation experiment on CoT and the coordinates of the anomalous area to prove the necessity of such a design. Additionally, the expression in lines 121 to 122 aims to reflect the importance of industrial anomaly detection, but it is indeed relatively unclear.

The expression in lines 224 to 227 of the paper is actually a specific explanation of the aforementioned filtering mechanism. Since there were obvious errors in the initially generated CoT and a large number of format non-compliant data, we first performed a format-based filtering. In the data with standard formats, we found that there were still logical errors such as the reasoning process not matching the final answer. Therefore, we further executed logic-based filtering. 

Finally, Figure 2 is a graphical description of the entire data set generation process. Through standardized manual annotation conducted on each sub-dataset separately, we completed the initial preparation of the samples. Then, we constructed challenging questions with distractors for each sample and combined the question results with accurate visual annotation information to form prompts. These prompts were input into the QwenVL-Max model to generate rigorous reasoning processes, which can be divided into three parts that perform different functions. Finally, the above filtering methods were executed on the generated CoT data, and after iterative updates, manual detection was conducted to eliminate possible errors. Thank you for pointing out these issues. We will correct them in the next version.

***The paper could benefit from some discussion about the relationship between visual-only methods (SPADE, PADIM, PatchCore, etc.) and VLLM-based methods.***

We agree with your point. Traditional IAD methods such as SPADE, PADIM, and PatchCore are generally based on pixel/feature reconstruction and feature embedding distance mechanisms, which can effectively handle texture/surface anomalies and perform well in controlled environments. However, these methods have limited capabilities in dealing with logical anomalies and are difficult to adapt to the multi-scene industrial environment. They usually require independent training models for each type of object, and most traditional IAD methods are only suitable for binary classification tasks of anomaly detection. In contrast, the VLLM-based approach possesses cross-modal generalization capabilities. In zero-shot scenarios, it enables collaborative visual and linguistic understanding to identify complex defects and infer their underlying causes. This flexibility in handling both anomaly detection and defect classification tasks significantly advances the application of IAD methods in practical environments. Thank you for pointing out these representative methods. We will add discussions about them in the next version.

***"CoT data undergoes Chinese character detection and missing coordinate detection" - why "Chinese character"?***

We utilized QwenVL-Max to generate initial CoT, and it is mainly pre-trained with Chinese and English corpora. Therefore, Chinese characters may be generated in the output, which is a phenomenon we do not expect.

Thanks again for the high-quality review. We hope our response could address your main concerns and we are happy to answer any further questions.

summary.value: This paper presents AnomalyCoT, a multimodal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) dataset for multi-scenario Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) tasks. Comprising 37,565 samples, the dataset integrates 13 public datasets and introduces structured CoT reasoning with precise anomaly region coordinates. Experiments show that fine-tuning Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) on AnomalyCoT significantly improves accuracy (up to 97.46%) and localization metrics, outperforming direct evaluations. The dataset addresses limitations of existing IAD datasets by enhancing scenario diversity, task complexity, and interpretability, demonstrating its utility for real-world MLLM applications in quality control.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. AnomalyCoT is the first multimodal CoT dataset for IAD, integrating diverse scenarios and structured reasoning, which fills a critical gap in existing IAD datasets that lack rigorous reasoning processes.
2. The paper conducts extensive experiments on various MLLMs, including both commercial and open-source models, and evaluates performance using multiple metrics (accuracy, IoU, GIoU, DIoU), providing a thorough benchmark.
3. Fine-tuning on AnomalyCoT leads to substantial improvements (average 36.5% accuracy boost), demonstrating the dataset's effectiveness in enhancing MLLMs' anomaly detection and localization capabilities.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. This paper focuses on MLLMs but lacks comparison with state-of-the-art traditional IAD methods, which could better contextualize the dataset's impact on the field.
2. While integrating multiple datasets, the paper does not explicitly address potential biases in source data distributions, which may affect generalizability to certain industrial sectors.
3. The test set's composition, including scene distribution and defect type proportions, is not explicitly described in the paper, and the evaluation metrics differ from traditional IAD methods' metrics, limiting comprehensive comparisons with specialized approaches.

summary.value: This paper introduces AnomalyCoT, a novel and large-scale multimodal dataset for Industrial Anomaly Detection, which contains 37,565 samples across 59 diverse industrial scenarios. What sets AnomalyCoT apart from previous IAD datasets is its rich Chain-of-Thought annotations. For each sample, the dataset provides not only a label but also a detailed reasoning process that includes analysis of incorrect options, identification of the correct defect, precise bounding box coordinates for the anomaly, and a plausible cause analysis. The authors demonstrate the value of their dataset through extensive experiments. They benchmark a range of state-of-the-art Multimodal Large Language Models, showing that while these models struggle with the task in a zero-shot setting, fine-tuning them on AnomalyCoT leads to dramatic and significant improvements in both classification accuracy and localization IoU.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. AnomalyCoT is the first to provide a structured, interpretable reasoning framework via Chain-of-Thought. This shifts the task from simple classification to a more complex and practical reasoning process, which is crucial for building trust and reliability in real-world IAD applications.

2. The scale and diversity of AnomalyCoT are impressive. By aggregating and unifying 13 public datasets and adding 4 new ones, the authors have created a benchmark that covers a wide variety of materials, defect types, and scenarios

3. The experimental results provide compelling evidence for the dataset's effectiveness. The stark contrast in performance between pre-trained and fine-tuned models is a powerful testament to what the dataset enables. The ablation studies are well-designed, clearly demonstrating that both the natural language reasoning and the precise spatial coordinates are critical components for achieving top performance.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper evaluates the models' performance, achieving impressive accuracy (e.g., up to 97.46%). However, it lacks a comparison to human expert performance on the same dataset. Such a baseline would be invaluable for contextualizing the results. It would help to understand whether the fine-tuned models are approaching, meeting, or exceeding the capabilities of human inspectors, especially on a task that is designed to emulate human-like reasoning via CoT. This comparison would provide a clearer picture of the practical significance of the achieved accuracy.

2. The CoT annotations were generated using a single powerful model, QwenVL-Max. While effective, this raises a minor methodological question about whether the dataset might be subtly biased towards the reasoning style or knowledge of this specific model family. Although the strong performance of the fine-tuned Llama models mitigates this concern significantly, it is a potential limitation worth acknowledging.

title.value: AnomalyCoT: A Multi-Scenario Chain-of-Thought Dataset for Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract.value: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) is an indispensable quality control technology in modern production processes. Recently, on account of the outstanding visual comprehension and cross-domain knowledge transfer capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), existing studies have explored the application of MLLMs in the IAD domain and established some multimodal IAD datasets. However, although the latest datasets contain various fundamental IAD tasks, they formulate tasks in a general question-and-answer format lacking a rigorous reasoning process, and they are relatively limited in the diversity of scenarios, which restricts their reliability in practical applications. In this paper, we propose AnomalyCoT, a multimodal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) dataset for multi-scenario IAD tasks. It consists of 37,565 IAD samples with the CoT data and is defined by challenging composite IAD tasks. Meanwhile, the CoT data for each sample provides precise coordinates of anomaly regions, thereby improving visual comprehension of defects across different types. AnomalyCoT is constructed through a systematic pipeline and involves multiple manual operations. Based on AnomalyCoT, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of various mainstream MLLMs and fine-tuned representative models in different ways. The final results show that Gemini-2.0-flash achieved the best performance in the direct evaluation with an accuracy rate of 59.6\%, while Llama 3.2-Vision achieves the best performance after LoRA fine-tuning with an accuracy rate of 94.0\%. Among all the fine-tuned models, the average accuracy improvement reaches 36.5\%, demonstrating the potential of integrating CoT datasets in future applications within the IAD field. The code and data are available at \url{https://github.com/Zhaolutuan/AnomalyCoT}.

pdf.description: Upload your submission as a PDF file that ends with .pdf. In this file the main text (max. nine pages), references, and checklist may be followed by technical appendices, for which there is no page limit. Paper PDF can be updated until the full paper submission deadline (May 15).

dataset_submission.description: Indicate whether your submission includes a dataset. **If you check this box, you must provide a valid Croissant metadata file and a URL to your dataset accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** For detailed requirements, please refer to the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines).

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
